8-Bit Hordes 8/10
The base gameplay in Hordes is the same as the rest of Petroglyph's "8-bit" line, so expect to play something that feels loosely like Command and Conquer, but this time with a bit of WarCraft mixed in. Unfortunately a lot of the issues with pathfinding, destroying terrain, workers going insane, etc, do persist as well. The positives also carry over. For a lower budget game, the micro in more open spaces works fine, hotkeying through big deathballs works well, and the C&C type UI is extremely intuitive, especially for newer players.

The campaign takes place after 8-Bit armies, and has some of the same drawbacks(lack of production value, no real story, no cutscenes, but there are a lot of scenarios to play through, and trying for 3 stars on all the missions is pretty engaging, and gave me good reason to go back and retry earlier levels. The benefits from 3 staring the missions are ridiculously overpowering, however, for some missions like the finale of the Lightbringer(humans) campaign, it's probably worth it. If you're newer to RTS games, I would like to note that there isn't really a perceptible difference between normal and hard difficulty. Getting bronze on most missions is very easy, but even during a few missions on the standard difficulty for the Lightbringers, you'll hit inconsistent challenge spikes that aren't mitigated by dropping difficulty. You'll be able to finish everything in the game without issue, just know that things might get grindy or attritional at times, and not in the best way. For the most part, though, the missions are good.

I originally got this game and played with my friends back in the day when I was in high school, it was fun for a time. It had some pretty animations, was just polished enough to feel mostly complete without feeling like you were missing to much, but that there might be more coming. Unit types felt at first like that mattered and seemed varied and interesting enough at first as well. 

Overtime as we played though my friends and I started to see just how shallow the game really was, there is no depth or strategy to the game whatsoever. In fact the straight up best faction or factions in the game are the marines and aliens mostly the aliens. The reason being that since the best and only strategy for this game is build up the largest splash damaging army possibly nothing else really matters. 

Regular Armies faction cant build to the same massive size but may start a little quicker than the space factions, and the Medieval factions build the fastest but are absolutely terrible late game due to population limits, so if you end up facing a Space faction as anything other than a space faction you are basically guaranteed to lose.

Worst part yet is the fact that they charge $45 for all 3 "games" each one is $15 for a campaign and 2 factions that are largely the same once you realize how little anything matters. They are in essence all just a reskin with slightly different buffs to each team. Which keep in mind players were asking for Naval armies or units for each faction and the EXCUSE given for us not receiving them?

"They would just be a reskin of some other army or unit" 

As if every faction isnt already basically a reskin with only 1 or 2 ACTUALLY useful SPLASH units you will literally use nothing else besides your splash spam unit that is it.

I saw they recently are coming out with 9 bit armies which to say is a disappointment is an understatement. All the things they could have added to this "$45 game" instead went into making another reskin of this for an even WORSE price of $20. Im not supporting greedy devs like this when all the suggestions and support from the community and their response is to lock content in this manner.

Overall there was a lot of potential for these games and had it been say $30 for all the factions together in ONE game id say it would be alittle more worth it. As it is though its just a very boring, short and disappointing game over all. 

These devs abandoned these 3 games already so theres no reason they wont abandon the next 9 bit armies once release is up. Not worth buying anything 

TLDR: Game is a shallow RTS with no strategy the best faction is Space dont buy anything else. Also they remade the exact same game but "newer" with the features players actually wanted for $20 (still not worth buying),

[h1]“While money can't buy happiness, it certainly lets you choose your own form of misery.”
~[i]Groucho Marx[/i][/h1]

There's nothing as sad as seeing one of your most favorite video game developers falling. And [i]man[/i], [b]Westwood Studios[/b] sure fell. Like many other legendary developers (including [b]Bullfrog Productions[/b], creators of [b]Populous[/b], [b]Syndicate[/b], [b]Theme Park[/b] and [b]Dungeon Keeper[/b], and [b]ORIGIN Systems[/b], creators of [b]Ultima[/b], [b]Wing Commander[/b] and [b]Crusader[/b]), [b]Westwood Studios[/b] was killed by [b]Electronic Arts[/b]. You don't need glasses to see why [b]EA[/b] wanted the guys. [b]The Legend of Kyrandia[/b], [b]Dune II[/b], [b]Lands of Lore[/b], [b]Blade Runner[/b], [b]NOX[/b] and, of course, [b]Command & Conquer[/b] were [i]huge[/i] names back in the days. Heck, according to statistics, [b]Westwood[/b] games had about [b]6%[/b] of the entire market. [i]Of course[/i], [b]EA[/b] wanted that. But what did [b]EA[/b] do after purchasing [b]Westwood[/b]? They did exactly what they usually do. They've put a lot of pressure on them (even though [b]Joe Bostic[/b] claimed that they didn't interfere in the process directly, you can totally see that their games under [b]EA[/b] were pretty rushed and we all know that [b]EA[/b] killed a lot of good projects by rushing the developers, [b]Anthem[/b] is a nice example of that) and then just closed them in early [b]2003[/b].

Naturally, I was really excited when part of the ex-[b]Westwood[/b] employees (including designer [b]Joe Bostic[/b]) founded [b]Petroglyph Games[/b]. [b]Mr. Bostic[/b] was there, [b]Michael Legg[/b] (who coded [b]The Legend of Kyrandia[/b] and [b]Blade Runner[/b]) was there and, of course, [b]Frank Klepacki[/b], one of my most favorite [b]VG[/b] composers of all times, was there too. Like I said, I was really excited. And you know what? [b]Petroglyph[/b]'s first game was pretty good. Sure, [b]Star Wars: Empire at War[/b] wasn't the very best [b]RTS[/b] ever made, [i]but[/i], like I said, it was good and gave me a lot of hope for the future. Unfortunately, right after that, things started to fall apart. After their next two games ([b]Universe at War: Earth Assault[/b] and [b]Panzer General: Allied Assault[/b]) received mediocre feedback, [b]Petroglyph[/b] started to release all sorts of crap. From ultra-cheap games that felt almost like scam ([b]Guardians of Graxia[/b] is a nice example of that) to [b]f2p[/b] nonsense with pay-to-win microtransactions. Like [b]Victory Command[/b]. And like I said at the very beginning of this review, it was really, [i]really[/i] sad to listen to [b]Frank Klepacki[/b]'s music while playing all that garbage. Good Lord, [b]f2p[/b] crap with the music from [b]Frank Klepacki[/b] himself... The man who composed [b]Act On Instinct[/b], [b]Hell March[/b] and one of my most favorite [b]VG[/b] tracks of all times – [b]Huline Jungle[/b] from [b]Lands of Lore: Guardians of Destiny[/b]... [i]Good grief[/i]...

Anyway, you've got the idea. At this point, [b]Petroglyph[/b] is nothing like [b]Westwood[/b]. They're terrible, [i]terrible[/i] developer that makes all sorts of crap. And here comes exactly that – yet another form of crap – shovelware. Sure, [b]8-bit Hordes[/b] doesn't look that bad. And let's just admit it - “[b]8-bit[/b]” stuff sells. That's pretty much the idea. Everybody loves [b]80[/b]s. Old farts like yours truly love such stuff because it reminds them of their youth, the new generation loves those because of a pretty cool “retro” aftertaste (say whatever you want, but there's a certain magic in [b]80[/b]s that appeals to pretty much everybody) that makes everything better... Like I said, [b]80[/b]s sell. Not only in video games. On big screen (I think everybody saw [b]8-bit Christmas[/b] during the holidays?), in [b]TV[/b] format ([b]Stranger Things[/b]), in comics ([b]Brian K. Vaughan[/b]'s [b]Paper Girls[/b] is one of the very best things I've read lately) and so on. And even though what we've got here is a [b]3D[/b] title that looks more like [b]3D Dot Game Heroes[/b] than real [b]8-bit[/b], let's just admit it – the game looks pretty tempting. Right?

Unfortunately, [b]8-bit Hordes[/b] is not nearly as good as it looks. And the first reason for that is the fact that... it's a scam. Simple like that. [b]Petroglyph[/b]'s “[b]8-bit[/b]” series is a shameless scam. Quite a lot of publishers are trying to sell us the same game more than once. [b]Nintendo[/b] is selling their retro stuff again and again in every generation, there are always those “retro collections” like [b]Mega Man Legacy Collection[/b], there are all sorts of remasters (including pretty basic ones like [b]Shenmue[/b]) and so on. But [b]Petroglyph[/b]? [b]Petroglyph[/b] decided to do even worse than that. They literally made one game and sold it to us three times. How? Easy. After finishing the game, they've made three basic “skins” for it. [b]8-bit Armies[/b] got [b]Command & Conquer[/b]-like look, [b]8-bit Hordes[/b] got fantasy look, while [b]8-bit Invaders![/b] (note the exclamation mark, [b]Sid Meier[/b] with his [b]Pirates![/b] sure approve) got aliens. End of the story. All three are [i]exactly[/i] the same game. I'm not overreacting, I'm not exaggerating, I'm not saying that just to make my review more funny. It's [i]the[/i]... same... exact... game. Just with different visuals. And there's a nice word for such stuff – [i]scam[/i].

But OK, OK, maybe it's a good game? Maybe having more of it is actually a good thing? Of course not. What we've got is an ultra-cheap [b]RTS[/b] that feels almost like mobile game. It's so basic, cheap and unsatisfying that it was hard to force myself to keep playing, even though I'm a huge [b]RTS[/b] geek and more [b]RTS[/b] is always welcomed by me. But honestly, [b]8-bit Hordes[/b] is just so slow and cheap and... ew. Just ew. I've played some one-man titles that felt [i]way[/i] better than this. [b]Marcell Baranyai[/b]'s [b]BC Kings[/b] for example. Made by one man, way better game. [i]Way[/i] better. The worst thing about [b]8-bit Hordes[/b], though, is its “optional” objectives. That thing pretty much killed [b]8-bit Armies[/b]. It was [i]so-o-o[/i] obvious that it broke the entire balance and it was obvious that it needed to be fixed, but since nobody really cared about the actual product and all [b]Petroglyph[/b] wanted is to sell us [b]8-bit Armies[/b] again without doing any work at all, they didn't bother to do anything about it. So, what's the problem? The problem is – every mission in this game (excluding tutorial) come with two “optional” objectives. Doesn't sound bad so far, but the thing is – those optional objectives are the only way to unlock new structures and units. Simple like that – you missed one of the “optional” objectives during the mission – you'll miss something important for the rest of the game. In other words, those “optional” objectives aren't really optional and end up being a huge pain in the butt.

All in all, though, this game doesn't even worth talking about. Like any other shovelware out there. It's close to impossible to consider this game as a real deal. Just because it's way too obvious that [b]Petroglyph[/b] didn't even try this time. Like the rest of [b]Petroglyph[/b]'s “[b]8-bit[/b]” games, [b]8-bit Hordes[/b] feels like one of those cheap mobile games that you pick up just because of nostalgia and then uninstall after a couple of minutes because of how unsatisfying it is. It's a bad game. Dull, cheap and uninspired. But the worst thing is? The worst thing is that it's from [b]Petroglyph[/b]. Seeing ex-[b]Westwood[/b] guys falling so low? It's sad. And the fact that [b]Frank Klepacki[/b]'s soundtrack for this game is very nice? It only makes things worse. People who worked on bloody [b]Dune II[/b] and [b]Command & Conquer[/b] wasting their lives on cheap shovelware scam? It's sad. I'm sad, guys. And nothing can cheer me up. Is that a cake?

Feels too much like a watered down RTS.  You can only build one unit at a time.  Units often get confused and don't do what you told them to do.  The main thing this game does right is with single player progression.  Beating levels and challenges give you bonus resources so that you can start the next playthrough faster.  The first level you start with a single worker and base.  Then as you move through you start with more initial workers, buildings, etc...  It nicely solves the problem of starting a base from scratch too many times while giving you a reason to do level challenges.

But, it still wasn't enough to make it fun.  There is no story to speak of, and each level's tasks weren't very good.  It all just felt bland and was missing some of the core stuff I have come to expect from even decades old RTS games.  One cool new feature doesn't fix the lack of a decent single player campaign or proper base building.

Per questa recensione, vi invito a cercavri 8-Bit Armies e 8-Bit Invaders; tutte appartenenti alla stessa serie, ognuna delle quali è di fatto un pacchetto di 2 Fazioni affini tra loro.

In questo caso, il discorso è opposto a quello fatto con le Fazioni di Invaders: ci vuole fegato per giocare le fazioni del pacchetto Hordes.

Entrambe le parti possiedono un campionario di unità ed edifici speciali molto particolare, con sinergie e tattiche tutt'altro che immediate. E sopratutto molto volubili a seconda della fazione che dovranno affrontare (ad esempio le unità dei lancieri sarebbero completamente inutili contro le unità cingolate di una delle fazioni Armies, dato che queste possono letteralmente camminare sulle orde di fantini costretti al corpo a corpo).

Oltre a ciò, le due fazioni Hordes devono sottostare a due importanti svantaggi:
-Le due fazioni contano su tanti raccoglitori, più economici (e fragili) delle altre fazioni. Il che richiede una maggiore accortezza nel calcolare come ottimizzare il numero di raccoglitori in proporzione alla possibilità di raggiungere nuovi giacimenti. E sopratutto, come accennato, sono molto più vulnerabili ai raid nemici: se un manipolo di truppe base non può da sola abbattere un "normale" raccoglitore, con i raccoglitori Hordes questo pericolo è presente.

-Al posto delle centrali elettriche delle fazioni Armies, gli Hordes devono costruire le Fattorie: ogni Fattoria permette la costruzione di 20 unità addizionali (essendo un gioco molto semplice, non si sono presi lo scomodo di far sì che alcune unità gravino maggiormente di altre su questo limite). Una seccatura da tenere bene a mente, sopratutto considerando che le unità delle due fazioni non sono tanto forti da compensare questo svantaggio.

-Difetto Bonus: le superarmi non sono niente di che...

Davvero due Fazioni di difficile utilizzo, sopratutto contro i colleghi overpower del pacchetto Invader. Confesso che sono le due fazioni che uso meno spesso.
Buona fortuna ad usarle.
